Assuming senior engineers code 10x faster rather than making better architectural decisions
Believing technical leads only manage people without technical depth
follow_up_questions: What does it mean for an engineer to be a 'team multiplier'?
How do the engineering expectations change when moving from campus hire to mid-level?

questions.question: How do you stay up-to-date with fast-evolving technologies in software engineering and AI?
questions.reference_answer: Interviewer is assessing: intellectual curiosity, self-directed learning, and personal information filtering. Technology evolves rapidly, especially in AI and web frameworks. Outline a disciplined learning routine: 1) Primary Sources: reading official documentation, release notes, and engineering blogs from top tech companies (Meta Engineering, Uber Engineering, Netflix TechBlog), 2) Hands-On Building: building small weekend projects or testing new libraries rather than just reading passively, 3) Curated Newsletters & Communities: Hacker News, GitHub Trending, arXiv papers, and reputable technical newsletters (ByteByteGo, Pragmatic Engineer), and 4) Podcasting / Technical Talks: watching conference talks (PyCon, AWS re:Invent). Illustrative example (replace with your routine): 'I follow engineering blogs like Uber and Cloudflare to understand real-world scale architectures, and I reserve 3 hours every weekend to build small experiments testing new tools like FastAPI or LangChain.'
key_points: Curated high-signal sources: official docs and top engineering tech blogs
Hands-on implementation over passive video watching
Disciplined weekly routine for exploring new tools
Focus on enduring foundational principles (networking, databases, OS) alongside hype tools
common_mistakes: Relying exclusively on 30-second TikTok or Instagram coding reels for technical knowledge
Chasing every single new hype library without understanding core computer science fundamentals
Claiming 'I don't need to learn anything new because college taught me everything'
follow_up_questions: How do you filter high-signal engineering content from shallow marketing hype?
What is one technical book or engineering article that fundamentally changed how you think?

questions.question: What would you do if you were assigned a legacy codebase with zero documentation, spaghetti code, and no unit tests?
questions.reference_answer: Interviewer is assessing: resilience, methodical reverse-engineering, and working with imperfect real-world systems. Most enterprise software is legacy. Strategy: 1) Resist the urge to rewrite: complete rewrites introduce massive regressions and cost millions, 2) Map the system: trace entry points (routes, controllers), set up logging, and map input-output boundaries, 3) Characterization Tests: write black-box end-to-end integration tests that capture CURRENT behavior (even bugs) to create a safety net before touching code, 4) Boy Scout Rule: leave the code slightly cleaner than you found it on every ticket, refactoring incrementally within small, tested pull requests, and 5) Document as you go: write setup guides and architectural diagrams for the next engineer. Illustrative example (replace with your experience): 'When working on an inherited college project codebase with no docs, I first wrote end-to-end tests to establish a baseline of existing behavior. I then refactored one module at a time while adding docstrings, turning an unmaintainable script into a clean, testable system.'
key_points: Resist demanding an immediate full rewrite; respect business value of legacy code
Write Characterization Tests to capture current behavior before refactoring
Apply the Boy Scout Rule: clean up code incrementally during feature work
Document architecture, dependencies, and environment setup as you learn
common_mistakes: Demanding an immediate full rewrite from scratch (classic junior anti-pattern)
Refactoring large legacy modules without any automated tests, breaking production
Complaining endlessly about previous developers' code quality instead of improving it
follow_up_questions: What is a Characterization Test (Golden Master test) in legacy code refactoring?
What is the Strangler Fig pattern for incrementally replacing legacy systems?

questions.question: What is the importance of code reviews from the perspective of both the author and the reviewer?
questions.reference_answer: Code reviews are a vital quality gate and knowledge-sharing ritual: 1) Author Perspective: acts as a safety net catching edge cases, performance bugs, and security oversights before production; provides tailored mentorship from senior peers; forces the author to write clean, self-documenting code with clear PR descriptions. 2) Reviewer Perspective: helps maintain architectural consistency and coding standards across the repository; shares knowledge so multiple engineers understand the new code (increasing bus factor); offers opportunities to learn novel techniques from teammates. It fosters a collective ownership culture where the entire team is responsible for codebase health. Illustrative example (replace with your facts): In my project team, I addressed this with proactive transparency and structured documentation.
key_points: Quality gate: catches bugs, security flaws, and performance regressions before deploy
Knowledge sharing: eliminates single points of failure (increases Bus Factor)
Mentorship vehicle for continuous engineering learning
Fosters collective code ownership rather than isolated silos
common_mistakes: Treating code reviews as a rubber-stamp approval without actually inspecting the code
Submitting massive 2,000-line pull requests that are impossible to review effectively
Using harsh, sarcastic, or demanding language in code review comments
follow_up_questions: What is an ideal pull request size to ensure thorough and effective code reviews?
What is the 'Bus Factor' in software engineering team resilience?

questions.question: What would you do if your software build fails or CI pipeline breaks right before a scheduled team demo?
questions.reference_answer: Interviewer is assessing: emotional composure, triage under pressure, and pragmatic recovery. Panic worsens technical crises. Protocol: 1) Stay calm and communicate: inform the team lead immediately so expectations can be set, 2) Inspect CI logs: look at the exact failing step (lint error, failed unit test, missing environment variable, dependency timeout) to isolate the failure fast, 3) Revert to last green commit: if the fix is non-trivial, revert to the last passing build immediately rather than hacking code in panic, and 4) Demo from stable environment: conduct the demo using the stable staging environment or last verified build while debugging continues offline. Illustrative example (replace with your experience): 'When our build failed 15 minutes before our final project presentation due to an API timeout, I didn't panic. I checked the logs, identified that a mock server was down, reverted to our local cache fixture, and delivered a smooth presentation without the evaluators ever knowing there was a crisis.'
key_points: Maintain emotional composure; panic creates careless mistakes
Inspect logs methodically to identify the exact failing step
Revert to the last known stable green build to secure the demo
Transparent communication with team lead regarding status
common_mistakes: Hacking code live on the main branch minutes before a presentation without testing
Freezing in panic and failing to notify the team
Blaming CI tools or teammates publicly
follow_up_questions: How do automated staging environments prevent demo day failures?
What is a 'pre-flight checklist' before presenting technical demos?

questions.question: How do you handle technical disagreements during sprint planning or architectural discussions?
questions.reference_answer: Interviewer is assessing: collaborative consensus-building and engineering maturity. Disagreements in system design are normal and healthy when handled constructively: 1) Ground arguments in objective criteria: evaluate options against specific project requirements (latency SLAs, development time, scalability, maintenance cost) rather than personal aesthetic preference, 2) Build quick Proof-of-Concepts (POCs): if the team is split between two architectures, spend a timeboxed 2-hour session benchmarking both with real data, 3) Involve senior guidance: present the trade-offs to the tech lead or architect for final arbitration, and 4) Commit fully: once a decision is finalized, execute the chosen architecture with full commitment without lingering resentment. Illustrative example (replace with your experience): 'When our team debated between SQL and MongoDB for our capstone database, we listed our data access patterns. Seeing that 90% of our queries required relational joins, the data clearly pointed to SQL, allowing us to align quickly without emotional arguments.'
key_points: Anchor debates in objective project requirements and performance metrics
Use quick, timeboxed Proof-of-Concepts (POCs) to let empirical data decide

questions.question: Write a Python function to check whether an integer is a palindrome without converting it to a string.
questions.reference_answer:
To check integer palindromes without string conversion, reverse the second half of the number mathematically and compare it with the first half:

```python
def is_palindrome_int(x: int) -> bool:
    if x < 0 or (x % 10 == 0 and x != 0):
        return False
    reversed_half = 0
    while x > reversed_half:
        reversed_half = reversed_half * 10 + x % 10
        x //= 10
    return x == reversed_half or x == reversed_half // 10
```

Sample Input: `121` -> Expected Output: `True`. Sample Input: `-121` -> Expected Output: `False`. Sample Input: `10` -> Expected Output: `False`. Negative numbers cannot be palindromes due to leading `-`. Reversing only half the digits prevents integer overflow. Time Complexity: O(log10(n)) proportional to digit count. Space Complexity: O(1) constant.
key_points: Negative numbers and non-zero multiples of 10 can never be palindromes
Reverse only the second half of the integer to avoid potential overflow
Middle digit in odd-length numbers is handled via `reversed_half // 10`
Time Complexity: O(log10(n)); Space Complexity: O(1)
common_mistakes: Converting integer to string `str(x) == str(x)[::-1]`, which violates the interview constraint
Forgetting that numbers ending in 0 (like 10, 100) are not palindromes except 0 itself
Reversing the entire 32-bit integer, risking overflow in languages like C/Java

```python
def reverse_words(s: str) -> str:
    words = s.split()
    return ' '.join(reversed(words))
```

questions.question: Write a Python function to find the missing number in an array containing distinct integers from 0 to n.
questions.reference_answer:
An array of length n contains distinct numbers from the range `[0, n]`. Exactly one number is missing. Method 1 (Summation formula): compute expected sum `n * (n + 1) // 2` and subtract the actual array sum in O(n) time and O(1) space. Method 2 (XOR bitwise approach): XOR all indices `0` to `n` with all array values; since `x ^ x = 0` and `x ^ 0 = x`, all pairs cancel out, leaving the missing number:

```python
def missing_number_xor(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    n = len(nums)
    missing = n
    for i, num in enumerate(nums):
        missing ^= i ^ num
    return missing
```

Sample Input: `[3, 0, 1]` -> Output: `2`. Sample Input: `[9,6,4,2,3,5,7,0,1]` -> Output: `8`. Time Complexity: O(n). Space Complexity: O(1). XOR avoids potential arithmetic overflow.
key_points: Gauss sum formula: `n * (n + 1) // 2` gives expected sum in O(1)
XOR property: `a ^ a = 0` and `a ^ 0 = a` cancels duplicates
XOR bitwise approach prevents integer overflow in fixed-width integer languages
Time Complexity: O(n); Space Complexity: O(1)
common_mistakes: Sorting the array first (O(n log n) time penalty)
Using a hash set lookup, consuming O(n) unnecessary auxiliary memory
Off-by-one errors in determining n (`len(nums)`)

questions.question: Write a Python function to find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters using the sliding window technique.
questions.reference_answer:
Using a sliding window with a dictionary storing the most recent index of each character allows computing the longest unique substring in a single linear pass:

```python
def length_of_longest_substring(s: str) -> int:
    char_index = {}
    max_len = 0
    start = 0
    for end, char in enumerate(s):
        if char in char_index and char_index[char] >= start:
            start = char_index[char] + 1
        char_index[char] = end
        max_len = max(max_len, end - start + 1)
    return max_len
```

When a duplicate character is encountered inside the current window (`char_index[char] >= start`), we shift the window `start` just past the duplicate's prior position. Sample Input: `s = "abcabcbb"` -> Output: `3` ("abc"). Sample Input: `s = "bbbbb"` -> Output: `1` ("b"). Sample Input: `s = "pwwkew"` -> Output: `3` ("wke"). Time Complexity: O(n) linear scan. Space Complexity: O(min(m, n)) where m is character set size.
key_points: Sliding window pattern with two pointers `start` and `end`
Hash map tracks character -> most recent index to skip repeated characters in O(1)
Condition `char_index[char] >= start` ensures we only shift forward if repeated char is inside the active window
Time Complexity: O(n); Space Complexity: O(min(m, n))
common_mistakes: Brute force checking all O(n^2) substrings with set validation in O(n^3) time

Failing on empty string or single-character string edge cases

questions.question: Write a Python function to calculate the factorial of a non-negative integer N iteratively and recursively.
questions.reference_answer:
Factorial of N (`N!`) is the product of all positive integers `<= N`; `0!` is defined as `1`. 1) Iterative implementation (O(n) time, O(1) space):

```python
def factorial_iterative(n: int) -> int:
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("Factorial undefined for negative numbers")
    result = 1
    for i in range(2, n + 1):
        result *= i
    return result
```

2) Recursive implementation: `return 1 if n <= 1 else n * factorial_recursive(n - 1)`. Sample Input: `5` -> `120`. Sample Input: `0` -> `1`. Iterative is preferred because it avoids Python's recursion limit for large inputs. In production, `math.factorial(n)` is C-optimized and significantly faster.

questions.question: Write a Python function to perform basic String Compression (Run-Length Encoding) using counts of repeated characters.
questions.reference_answer:
Run-length encoding compresses consecutive duplicate characters into character-count pairs (e.g., `"aabcccccaaa"` -> `"a2b1c5a3"`). Return original string if compressed string is not shorter:

```python
def compress_string(s: str) -> str:
    if not s:
        return ""
    compressed = []
    count = 1
    for i in range(1, len(s)):
        if s[i] == s[i - 1]:
            count += 1
        else:
            compressed.append(f"{s[i - 1]}{count}")
            count = 1
    compressed.append(f"{s[-1]}{count}")
    result = "".join(compressed)
    return result if len(result) < len(s) else s
```

Sample Input: `"aabcccccaaa"` -> Output: `"a2b1c5a3"`. Sample Input: `"abcdef"` -> Output: `"abcdef"` (compressed `"a1b1c1d1e1f1"` is longer). Time Complexity: O(n). Space Complexity: O(n).
key_points: Appends characters and run counts using a list before `"".join()` for O(n) time
Handles trailing character group after loop terminates
Returns original string if compressed length is not strictly shorter

questions.question: Write a Python function to rotate a list of N integers to the right by K steps in-place.
questions.reference_answer:
Rotating an array right by K steps can be achieved in O(n) time and O(1) space using the Three-Step Array Reversal algorithm: 1) Normalize `k = k % len(nums)`, 2) Reverse the entire array, 3) Reverse the first `k` elements, 4) Reverse the remaining `n - k` elements:

```python
def rotate(nums: list[int], k: int) -> None:
    n = len(nums)
    k = k % n
    def reverse(start: int, end: int) -> None:
        while start < end:
            nums[start], nums[end] = nums[end], nums[start]
            start += 1
            end -= 1
    reverse(0, n - 1)      # Reverse entire array
    reverse(0, k - 1)      # Reverse first k elements
    reverse(k, n - 1)      # Reverse remaining elements
```

Sample Input: `nums = [1,2,3,4,5,6,7], k = 3` -> Output: `[5,6,7,1,2,3,4]`. Time Complexity: O(n). Space Complexity: O(1) strictly in-place.
key_points: Normalize k: `k = k % n` handles k larger than array length
Three-step reversal: reverse all -> reverse first k -> reverse remainder
Time Complexity: O(n); Space Complexity: O(1) in-place
Avoids allocating auxiliary array
common_mistakes: Rotating 1 step k times sequentially in a loop, resulting in O(n * k) slow time
Forgetting `k = k % n`, causing IndexError when k exceeds array length

questions.question: Write a Python function to merge two sorted integer lists into a single sorted list in O(n + m) time.
questions.reference_answer:
Using two pointers achieves optimal O(n + m) linear time without sorting:

```python
def merge_sorted_lists(l1: list[int], l2: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    merged = []
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(l1) and j < len(l2):
        if l1[i] <= l2[j]:
            merged.append(l1[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            merged.append(l2[j])
            j += 1
    merged.extend(l1[i:])
    merged.extend(l2[j:])
    return merged
```

Compare current elements `l1[i]` and `l2[j]`. Append the smaller element to `merged` and advance its pointer. Once one list is exhausted, append remaining elements of the other list. This is the core merge step of MergeSort. Sample Input: `l1 = [1, 2, 4], l2 = [1, 3, 4]` -> Output: `[1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4]`. Time Complexity: O(n + m). Space Complexity: O(n + m).
key_points: Two-pointer comparison traverses both lists simultaneously
Appends remaining elements via `.extend()` after one list is exhausted
Core merge routine used in Merge Sort and external sorting
Time Complexity: O(n + m); Space Complexity: O(n + m)
common_mistakes: Concatenating lists and calling `sorted(l1 + l2)` (O((n+m) log(n+m)) time penalty)
Missing elements from the longer list when the while loop terminates
Using `<=` comparison preserves sorting stability for equal elements

questions.question: Explain Bubble Sort, Selection Sort, and Insertion Sort. Compare their time and space complexities.
questions.reference_answer: 1) Bubble Sort: repeatedly steps through the list, compares adjacent elements, and swaps them if in wrong order. Largest unsorted element 'bubbles up' to the end on each pass. Best: O(n) with swap flag; Average/Worst: O(n^2); Space: O(1); Stable. 2) Selection Sort: repeatedly finds minimum element from unsorted portion and swaps it with the first unsorted position. Makes minimum number of writes (at most n swaps). Best/Average/Worst: O(n^2) always; Space: O(1); Unstable. 3) Insertion Sort: iterates through array, picking current element and inserting it into its correct sorted position among previously scanned elements. Excellent for small or nearly sorted arrays. Best: O(n); Average/Worst: O(n^2); Space: O(1); Stable.
key_points: Bubble Sort: adjacent swaps; O(n^2) time, O(1) space; stable
Selection Sort: finds minimum and swaps; O(n^2) always, minimum writes; unstable
Insertion Sort: shifts elements to insert; O(n) best case on nearly sorted data; stable
All three have O(1) constant auxiliary space
common_mistakes: Assuming Selection Sort is stable (swapping can move duplicate elements across each other)
Forgetting the early-exit optimization flag in Bubble Sort for already-sorted lists
Using O(n^2) elementary sorts on large datasets (> 10,000 elements)
follow_up_questions: Why is Insertion Sort used as the base case in hybrid algorithms like Timsort for small partitions (n <= 32)?

questions.question: Explain Merge Sort and Quick Sort. What are their average and worst-case complexities, and when is each preferred?
questions.reference_answer: 1) Merge Sort: Divide-and-Conquer algorithm that divides array into two halves, recursively sorts them, and merges sorted halves. Guranteed O(n log n) time in best, average, and worst cases. Stable sort. Disadvantage: requires O(n) auxiliary memory for merge buffers. Preferred for linked lists and external disk sorting. 2) Quick Sort: Divide-and-Conquer algorithm that selects a 'pivot' element, partitions array such that elements smaller than pivot are on left and larger on right, and recursively sorts partitions. Average time: O(n log n); Worst case: O(n^2) when pivot selection is poor (e.g., sorted array with first element as pivot). Unstable sort. Advantage: O(log n) in-place space, excellent cache locality, faster in practice on arrays.
key_points: Merge Sort: guaranteed O(n log n) best/average/worst; O(n) space; stable
Quick Sort: O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst case; O(log n) space in-place; unstable
Quick Sort preferred for in-memory array sorting due to cache locality
Merge Sort preferred for linked lists and external sorting where stable O(n log n) is needed
common_mistakes: Selecting the first element as pivot in Quick Sort on sorted inputs (triggers worst-case O(n^2) time)
Assuming Quick Sort requires O(1) space (recursive call stack requires O(log n) space)
Believing Merge Sort can be easily performed in-place on arrays without complex overhead
follow_up_questions: How does Median-of-Three or randomized pivot selection prevent Quick Sort's O(n^2) worst case?

questions.question: Explain Heap Sort and Priority Queues. What are the time complexities for insertion, deletion, and heapify?
questions.reference_answer: A Binary Heap is a complete binary tree satisfying the Heap Property: in a Min-Heap, each parent node is `<= ` its children (root is minimum); in a Max-Heap, each parent is `>=` its children (root is maximum). Array representation: for node at index `i`, left child is `2i + 1`, right child is `2i + 2`, and parent is `(i - 1) // 2`. Operations: 1) `Insert (heappush)`: append to end and bubble up; O(log n). 2) `Extract Min/Max (heappop)`: replace root with last element and bubble down (sift down); O(log n). 3) `Build Heap (heapify)`: converts unorganized array of N elements into a valid heap in O(n) linear time. Heap Sort builds a Max-Heap and repeatedly swaps root with end, achieving guaranteed O(n log n) time and O(1) in-place auxiliary space.
key_points: Heap property: parent is always <= (min-heap) or >= (max-heap) children
Binary heap mapped compactly into flat array using index arithmetic
Heapify constructs a heap from unsorted array in O(n) linear time
Heap Sort: guaranteed O(n log n) time in all cases with O(1) auxiliary space
common_mistakes: Assuming building a heap of N elements takes O(N log N) (it takes O(N) due to mathematical series convergence)
Confusing a Binary Heap with a Binary Search Tree (heap has no left < right ordering)
Using standard sorting when a Priority Queue is only querying top-K elements

questions.question: Explain the Tower of Hanoi mathematical puzzle. Write a recursive Python solution and state its complexity.
questions.reference_answer:
The Tower of Hanoi consists of three rods (Source, Target, Auxiliary) and N disks of different sizes. Rules: 1) Move one disk at a time, 2) Only the top disk can be moved, 3) No disk may be placed on top of a smaller disk. Recursive strategy: to move N disks from Source to Target: a) Move N-1 disks from Source to Auxiliary, b) Move N-th (largest) disk directly from Source to Target, c) Move N-1 disks from Auxiliary to Target:

```python
def tower_of_hanoi(n: int, source: str, target: str, auxiliary: str) -> None:
    if n == 1:
        print(f"Move disk 1 from {source} to {target}")
        return
    tower_of_hanoi(n - 1, source, auxiliary, target)
    print(f"Move disk {n} from {source} to {target}")
    tower_of_hanoi(n - 1, auxiliary, target, source)
```
Total moves required: `2^N - 1`. Time Complexity: O(2^N) exponential. Space Complexity: O(N) call stack depth.
key_points: Divide problem into three recursive steps
Base case: `n == 1` moves single disk directly to target
Total moves required is strictly `2^N - 1`
Time Complexity: O(2^N); Space Complexity: O(N) call stack
common_mistakes: Confusing target and auxiliary rods in the second recursive call
Forgetting the base case n=1
Attempting to solve for N > 30, which requires billions of operations

questions.question: Write a Python function to calculate `pow(x, n)` (x raised to the power n) in O(log n) time using Binary Exponentiation.
questions.reference_answer:
Naive multiplication `x * x * ... * x` takes O(n) time. Binary Exponentiation (Exponentiation by Squaring) computes `x^n` in O(log n) time using properties: if n is even, `x^n = (x^2)^(n/2)`; if n is odd, `x^n = x * (x^2)^((n-1)/2)`:

```python
def my_pow(x: float, n: int) -> float:
    if n < 0:
        x = 1 / x
        n = -n
    result = 1.0
    current_product = x
    while n > 0:
        if n % 2 == 1:
            result *= current_product
        current_product *= current_product
        n //= 2
    return result
```

Sample Input: `x = 2.0, n = 10` -> Output: `1024.0`. Sample Input: `x = 2.0, n = -2` -> Output: `0.25`. Handles negative exponents and `n=0`. Time Complexity: O(log n). Space Complexity: O(1) iterative.
key_points: Binary exponentiation squares the base and halves the exponent at each step
Reduces multiplications from O(n) linear to O(log n) logarithmic
Handles negative exponents by inverting base `x = 1/x` and `n = -n`
Iterative implementation runs in O(1) auxiliary space
common_mistakes: Linear loop multiplying x by itself n times (too slow for large n)
Not handling negative exponents (e.g., 2^-2 = 0.25)

```python
def sum_of_digits(n: int) -> int:

```

questions.question: Explain the 3-liter and 5-liter Water Jug Puzzle to measure exactly 4 liters. What is the mathematical foundation (Bézout's identity)?
questions.reference_answer: Problem: You have an unmarked 3-liter jug, an unmarked 5-liter jug, and an unlimited water source. Measure exactly 4 liters. Solution: 1) Fill 5L jug completely (0, 5), 2) Pour from 5L into 3L jug until full, leaving 2L in 5L jug (3, 2), 3) Empty 3L jug (0, 2), 4) Pour the 2L from 5L jug into 3L jug (2, 0), 5) Fill 5L jug completely (2, 5), 6) Pour from 5L into 3L jug until 3L jug is full (needs 1L). The 5L jug now contains exactly 4 liters: `5 - 1 = 4L`. Mathematical foundation: Bézout's Identity states that for integers a and b, the equation `a*x + b*y = d` has integer solutions if and only if d is a multiple of `gcd(a, b)`. Since `gcd(3, 5) = 1`, any integer volume between 1 and 5 can be measured.

Can be modeled algorithmically as BFS in a state-space graph

questions.question: Explain the Monty Hall Probability Problem. Why should the contestant always switch doors?
questions.reference_answer: Problem: A game show has 3 doors. Behind one door is a car (prize); behind the other two are goats. You pick Door 1. The host (Monty Hall), who knows what is behind every door, opens Door 3, revealing a goat. He asks: 'Do you want to stick with Door 1 or switch to Door 2?' Mathematical analysis: 1) When you picked Door 1, your probability of picking the car was 1/3; the probability the car was behind Door 2 or 3 was 2/3. 2) Monty Hall is constrained: he ALWAYS opens a goat door. His action does not change your initial 1/3 probability on Door 1. Instead, the entire 2/3 probability of the unchosen doors concentrates onto the remaining unopened Door 2. 3) Switching wins the car 2/3 of the time; staying wins only 1/3 of the time. You should always switch.
key_points: Initial pick probability is 1/3; unpicked doors combine to 2/3 probability
Host's action is non-random: he always reveals a goat, concentrating 2/3 probability on the remaining door
Switching doubles winning chances from 33.3% to 66.7%

questions.question: What is Big-O, Big-Omega, and Big-Theta notation in asymptotic complexity analysis?
questions.reference_answer: Asymptotic notation characterizes algorithm efficiency as input size N grows toward infinity: 1) Big-O (`O(f(N))`): Asymptotic Upper Bound. Represents the worst-case growth rate; the algorithm will perform no worse than this bound: `T(N) <= c * f(N)` for large N. 2) Big-Omega (`Omega(f(N))`): Asymptotic Lower Bound. Represents the best-case growth rate; the algorithm will perform at least this well: `T(N) >= c * f(N)`. 3) Big-Theta (`Theta(f(N))`): Asymptotic Tight Bound. Applies when upper and lower bounds coincide; the algorithm grows precisely at this rate: `c1 * f(N) <= T(N) <= c2 * f(N)`. In industry interviews, developers colloquially say 'Big-O' when they technically refer to Big-Theta tight bounds of worst-case runtime.
key_points: Big-O: upper bound (worst-case ceiling; no worse than f(N))
Big-Omega: lower bound (best-case floor; at least f(N))
Big-Theta: tight bound (sandwiched between bounds; grows exactly as f(N))
Ignores constant factors and lower-order terms as N approaches infinity
common_mistakes: Including constant multipliers or lower-order terms (e.g., writing O(2N + 5) instead of O(N))
Confusing worst-case time with Big-O (Big-O is a mathematical bound, not a case)
Assuming O(1) means instantaneous (O(1) means constant operations, which could take 10 seconds)

questions.question: Explain Amortized Time Complexity with the example of dynamic array resizing (Python list `append`).
questions.reference_answer: Amortized analysis evaluates the average time per operation over a long sequence of operations, accounting for rare, expensive operations balanced by frequent, cheap operations. Dynamic Array Example (Python list / C++ std::vector): appending to an array with spare capacity takes O(1) time. When capacity is full, appending triggers a resize: 1) Allocate a new array double the capacity (2X), 2) Copy all N elements over (O(N) cost), 3) Append the new element. Although the resize operation takes O(N), it happens very infrequently (after 1, 2, 4, 8, 16... inserts). Averaged across all N inserts, total work is `N (cheap inserts) + 2N (copies) = 3N` operations, yielding `3N / N = O(1)` amortized time per append.
key_points: Amortized analysis averages cost over a sequence of operations
Python list `append()` is O(1) amortized, but occasionally O(N) worst-case during resize
Geometric doubling (e.g., 2X capacity) guarantees O(1) amortized cost
Arithmetic expansion (e.g., adding +10 slots) degrades amortized append to O(N)
common_mistakes: Claiming dynamic array append is strictly O(1) worst-case (it is O(N) worst-case during resize)
Thinking fixed-amount resizing (+100 items) is as efficient as doubling (it causes quadratic O(N^2) total time)
Confusing average-case complexity with amortized complexity

questions.question: What is the difference between Time Complexity and Space Complexity? What is Auxiliary Space?
questions.reference_answer: 1) Time Complexity: quantifies the number of basic operations (comparisons, arithmetic steps) executed by an algorithm as a function of input size N. 2) Space Complexity: quantifies the total memory required by the algorithm during execution, including input data storage. 3) Auxiliary Space: the extra or temporary memory allocated by the algorithm EXCLUDING the space taken by the input data itself. In interview coding, 'space complexity' almost always refers to Auxiliary Space. Example: finding the maximum element in an array of size N requires O(N) input space, but O(1) auxiliary space because it only uses a single tracking variable.
key_points: Time Complexity measures operation count growth relative to input size N
Space Complexity measures total memory consumption

questions.question: How do you detect and fix an off-by-one error (OBOE) in array iteration loops?
questions.reference_answer: An Off-By-One Error (OBOE) occurs when a loop iterates one time too many or one time too few, typically caused by incorrect boundary operators (`<` vs `<=`) or misunderstanding zero-based indexing. Classic manifestations: 1) `IndexError: list index out of range` when accessing `arr[len(arr)]` instead of `arr[len(arr) - 1]`, 2) Skipping the final boundary element by using `<` instead of `<=`, and 3) Range mismatches in Python's half-open intervals `range(start, stop)` where `stop` is exclusive. Debugging strategy: test boundary values (n=0, n=1, n=2, and last element), verify half-open interval conventions, and prefer pythonic iterators `for item in arr:` or `enumerate()` over manual index manipulation.

A1 is guaranteed the overall #1 fastest horse! D and E groups are eliminated entirely. C2 and C3 are eliminated (since C1 was 3rd). B3 is eliminated. 3) Race 7: race remaining contenders for 2nd and 3rd: {A2, A3, B1, B2, C1}. Top 2 finishers in Race 7 are the overall #2 and #3 horses. Exactly 7 races.

questions.question: How do you detect memory leaks in long-running Python programs using `tracemalloc`?
questions.reference_answer:
While Python uses automatic garbage collection, memory leaks occur when unused objects remain referenced by global variables, long-lived caches, circular closures, or unclosed file descriptors. The standard library `tracemalloc` module tracks memory allocations per code line:

```python
import tracemalloc

tracemalloc.start()
# execute suspicious workflow
snapshot1 = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
# execute workflow again
snapshot2 = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()

top_stats = snapshot2.compare_to(snapshot1, 'lineno')
for stat in top_stats[:5]:
    print(stat)
```
`compare_to()` highlights lines allocating growing memory buffers across iterations, pinpointing memory leaks.
key_points: `tracemalloc` traces memory allocations back to exact source code lines
Take snapshots before and after suspicious workflows to compare differences
Identifies leaks caused by unbounded caches, global lists, and lingering references
Low runtime overhead suitable for staging diagnostics

questions.question: What is the difference between a shallow bug and a heisenbug in software engineering?
questions.reference_answer: 1) Bohrbug (Standard / Shallow Bug): a reproducible, deterministic bug that reliably manifests whenever a specific set of input conditions occurs, regardless of environment or debugging tools. Easily isolated and fixed using unit tests and debuggers. 2) Heisenbug: an elusive, non-deterministic bug that disappears or alters its behavior when an engineer attempts to observe or debug it (named after Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle). Common causes: race conditions in multithreaded code (adding `print()` or attaching a debugger changes thread timing, hiding the race), uninitialized memory in C/C++, compiler optimizations, or timing-dependent network socket delays. Resolving heisenbugs requires non-intrusive logging, stress testing, and concurrency analysis tools.

Heisenbug: disappears or mutates behavior when investigated or debugged

questions.question: Explain the Two-Pointer technique in array algorithms. What are the opposite-directional and same-directional patterns?
questions.reference_answer: The Two-Pointer technique optimizes nested-loop O(n^2) array problems into linear O(n) time by maintaining two index pointers: 1) Opposite-Directional (Converging): pointers start at opposite ends (`left = 0`, `right = len - 1`) and move toward each other based on comparison conditions. Used on sorted arrays (Two Sum II, Container With Most Water, Palindrome verification). 2) Same-Directional (Fast & Slow / Sliding Window): both pointers move in the same direction. Fast pointer scans while slow pointer tracks write positions or window boundaries (e.g., Move Zeroes, Remove Duplicates, Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters). Pointers advance conditionally, ensuring every element is visited a constant number of times.

questions.question: What is the Sliding Window algorithmic pattern? Contrast fixed-size vs dynamic-size sliding windows.
questions.reference_answer: The Sliding Window pattern maintains a contiguous sub-range of an array or string that slides across data to track metrics (sums, character counts) in O(n) time without recomputing from scratch: 1) Fixed-Size Window: window width K is constant. Initialize sum of first K elements. As window shifts right, add the incoming element and subtract the outgoing element in O(1): `window_sum += arr[i] - arr[i - K]`. Total time is O(n) vs O(n*k) brute force (e.g., Maximum sum subarray of size K). 2) Dynamic-Size Window: window expands by advancing right pointer until a condition is satisfied or violated, then contracts by advancing left pointer until condition restores (e.g., Smallest subarray with sum >= S, Longest substring with K distinct characters).
key_points: Fixed-size: add incoming element and subtract outgoing element in O(1)
Dynamic-size: expand right pointer, contract left pointer based on condition

Common auxiliary data structures: hash map or Counter to track window state
common_mistakes: Recalculating window sum from scratch on every step, degrading back to O(n*k)

questions.question: How do you systematically analyze and prove the Time and Space Complexity of a recursive algorithm?
questions.reference_answer: To analyze recursive complexity: 1) Formulate Recurrence Relation: express runtime `T(n)` in terms of subproblem sizes and non-recursive work. E.g., Merge Sort: `T(n) = 2*T(n/2) + O(n)`. 2) Solve Recurrence: a) Master Theorem: for `T(n) = a*T(n/b) + O(n^d)`, compare `log_b(a)` to `d`. If equal, `T(n) = O(n^d * log n)`. b) Recursion Tree Method: visualize call tree, compute work done per level, and sum across all tree levels (`height * work_per_level`). 3) Space Complexity: maximum depth of the recursion tree on the call stack multiplied by memory allocated per frame (e.g., O(n) for linear recursion, O(log n) for balanced divide-and-conquer). Memoization adds auxiliary cache memory.

questions.question: Write a Python function to invert a binary tree (swap left and right children for every node).
questions.reference_answer:
Inverting a binary tree swaps the left and right children of every node throughout the hierarchy:

```python
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def invert_tree(root: TreeNode | None) -> TreeNode | None:
    if not root:
        return None
    # Swap children
    root.left, root.right = root.right, root.left
    # Recurse on subtrees
    invert_tree(root.left)
    invert_tree(root.right)
    return root
```

Sample Input: `[4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6, 9]` -> Expected Output: `[4, 7, 2, 9, 6, 3, 1]`. Time Complexity: O(n) where n is the number of nodes (visits every node once). Space Complexity: O(h) where h is tree height for the recursion call stack (O(log n) for balanced tree, O(n) worst-case skewed tree). An iterative level-order traversal using `collections.deque` achieves identical O(n) time.

questions.question: Write a Python function to perform an Inorder Traversal of a Binary Tree iteratively using an explicit stack.

Inorder traversal visits nodes in the order Left -> Root -> Right. To perform this iteratively without recursion, an explicit LIFO stack simulates the call stack:

```python
def inorder_traversal(root: TreeNode | None) -> list[int]:
    result = []
    stack = []
    curr = root
    while curr or stack:
        # Reach the leftmost node of the current subtree
        while curr:
            stack.append(curr)
            curr = curr.left
        curr = stack.pop()
        result.append(curr.val)
        # Visit right subtree
        curr = curr.right
    return result
```

Sample Input: `[1, None, 2, 3]` -> Expected Output: `[1, 3, 2]`. On a Binary Search Tree (BST), inorder traversal always yields values in strictly ascending sorted order. Time Complexity: O(n) since every node is pushed and popped exactly once. Space Complexity: O(h) where h is tree height.

questions.question: Write a Python function to detect if a singly linked list has a cycle, and find the node where the cycle begins.
questions.reference_answer:
Floyd's Cycle-Finding Algorithm (Tortoise and Hare) detects cycles and identifies the cycle entry point in O(n) time and O(1) space:

```python
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next

def detect_cycle(head: ListNode | None) -> ListNode | None:
    slow = fast = head
    # Phase 1: Detect if a cycle exists
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow == fast:
            break
    else:
        return None  # No cycle found

    # Phase 2: Find the entry node of the cycle
    entry = head
    while entry != slow:
        entry = entry.next
        slow = slow.next
    return entry
```

Mathematical proof: if head-to-cycle length is `L`, and meeting point is `d` from entry inside cycle of length `C`, then `2*(L + d) = L + d + k*C` -> `L = k*C - d`. Moving one pointer from head and one from intersection point at equal 1-step speed meets precisely at the cycle entrance.
key_points: Phase 1: fast pointer advances 2 steps, slow pointer 1 step; they meet if cycle exists
Phase 2: reset entry pointer to head; advance both 1 step until they collide at cycle entry
Time Complexity: O(n); Space Complexity: O(1) strictly in-place
Mathematical relation: distance from head to entrance equals distance from meeting point to entrance

questions.question: Write a Python function to reverse a singly linked list both iteratively and recursively.
questions.reference_answer:
1) Iterative approach: maintain three pointers (`prev`, `curr`, `next_node`) and reverse links one by one in a single pass:

```python
def reverse_list_iterative(head: ListNode | None) -> ListNode | None:
    prev = None
    curr = head
    while curr:
        next_node = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = next_node
    return prev
```

2) Recursive approach:
```python
def reverse_list_recursive(head: ListNode | None) -> ListNode | None:
    if not head or not head.next:
        return head
    new_head = reverse_list_recursive(head.next)
    head.next.next = head
    head.next = None
    return new_head
```
Sample Input: `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5` -> Output: `5 -> 4 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1`. Iterative Time: O(n), Space: O(1). Recursive Time: O(n), Space: O(n) call stack.

Using a dummy node simplifies edge-case handling when stitching two sorted linked lists together:

```python
def merge_two_sorted_lists(l1: ListNode | None, l2: ListNode | None) -> ListNode | None:
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    tail = dummy
    while l1 and l2:
        if l1.val <= l2.val:
            tail.next = l1
            l1 = l1.next
        else:
            tail.next = l2
            l2 = l2.next
        tail = tail.next
    # Attach remaining non-empty list
    tail.next = l1 if l1 else l2
    return dummy.next
```

questions.question: Write a Python function to find a peak element in an array where nums[i] != nums[i+1] in O(log n) time.
questions.reference_answer:
A peak element is strictly greater than its neighbors. Binary search can find a peak in O(log n) by following the rising slope:

```python
def find_peak_element(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    low, high = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while low < high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        if nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]:
            # Upward slope: a peak must exist to the right
            low = mid + 1
        else:
            # Downward slope: mid itself or an element to the left is a peak
            high = mid
    return low
```

Logic: if `nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]`, we are on an ascending slope, guaranteeing at least one local peak exists in `[mid + 1, high]`. Otherwise, a peak exists in `[low, mid]`. Sample Input: `[1, 2, 3, 1]` -> Output: `2` (index of 3). Sample Input: `[1, 2, 1, 3, 5, 6, 4]` -> Output: `1` or `5`. Time Complexity: O(log n). Space Complexity: O(1).

questions.question: Write a Python function to solve the Container With Most Water problem in O(n) time.
questions.reference_answer:
The area between two vertical lines at indices `i` and `j` is given by `(j - i) * min(height[i], height[j])`. A two-pointer inward converging approach achieves O(n) linear time:

```python
def max_area(height: list[int]) -> int:
    left, right = 0, len(height) - 1
    max_water = 0
    while left < right:
        width = right - left
        current_water = width * min(height[left], height[right])
        if current_water > max_water:
            max_water = current_water
        # Move the pointer pointing to the shorter vertical bar
        if height[left] < height[right]:
            left += 1
        else:
            right -= 1
    return max_water
```

Greedy rationale: the width `(right - left)` shrinks on every step. To have any chance of finding a larger area, we must find a taller line, so we advance the pointer with the shorter bar. Sample Input: `[1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7]` -> Output: `49`. Time Complexity: O(n). Space Complexity: O(1).

questions.question: Write a Python function to validate a 9x9 Sudoku board according to standard rules.
questions.reference_answer:
A valid Sudoku board requires that numbers 1-9 occur without repetition across: 1) each row, 2) each column, and 3) each 3x3 sub-grid. Empty cells are represented by `'.'`. Hash sets track seen digits:

```python
def is_valid_sudoku(board: list[list[str]]) -> bool:
    rows = [set() for _ in range(9)]
    cols = [set() for _ in range(9)]
    boxes = [set() for _ in range(9)]
    for r in range(9):
        for c in range(9):
            val = board[r][c]
            if val == '.':
                continue
            box_idx = (r // 3) * 3 + (c // 3)
            if val in rows[r] or val in cols[c] or val in boxes[box_idx]:
                return False
            rows[r].add(val)
            cols[c].add(val)
            boxes[box_idx].add(val)
    return True
```

Box indexing formula: `(r // 3) * 3 + (c // 3)` uniquely maps each `(r, c)` cell into its respective 3x3 box numbered 0 to 8. Time Complexity: O(1) since board is fixed 9x9 (81 iterations). Space Complexity: O(1) bounded auxiliary sets.

```python
def min_cost_climbing_stairs(cost: list[int]) -> int:
    # prev2 is min cost to reach step i-2; prev1 is min cost to reach step i-1
    prev2, prev1 = cost[0], cost[1]
    for i in range(2, len(cost)):
        curr = cost[i] + min(prev1, prev2)
        prev2, prev1 = prev1, curr
    return min(prev1, prev2)
```

Recurrence relation: `dp[i] = cost[i] + min(dp[i-1], dp[i-2])`. At the top floor, we can step from `n-1` or `n-2`, so we return `min(prev1, prev2)`. Sample Input: `[10, 15, 20]` -> Output: `15`. Sample Input: `[1, 100, 1, 1, 1, 100, 1, 1, 100, 1]` -> Output: `6`. Time Complexity: O(n). Space Complexity: O(1).
key_points: Recurrence: `dp[i] = cost[i] + min(dp[i-1], dp[i-2])`
Base cases: start at index 0 with cost[0] or index 1 with cost[1]
Space optimization: keep only previous two states (`prev1`, `prev2`)
Time Complexity: O(n); Space Complexity: O(1)
common_mistakes: Allocating a full DP table of size N when only two variables are required
Returning `cost[-1]` instead of `min(prev1, prev2)` for the final step past the array
Using naive recursion without memoization (O(2^n) time)

How do you reconstruct the actual path of steps taken to achieve minimum cost?

questions.question: Write a Python function to solve the Coin Change problem (minimum coins to make up an amount) using Dynamic Programming.
questions.reference_answer:
Given integer array `coins` and integer `amount`, return the fewest coins needed, or `-1` if amount cannot be made. Unbounded knapsack dynamic programming:

```python
def coin_change(coins: list[int], amount: int) -> int:
    dp = [float('inf')] * (amount + 1)
    dp[0] = 0  # 0 coins to make amount 0
    for c in coins:
        for a in range(c, amount + 1):
            dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1)
    return dp[amount] if dp[amount] != float('inf') else -1
```

Recurrence: `dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - coin] + 1)`. We initialize `dp` with infinity. Iterating coins first or amount first both work for minimum count. Sample Input: `coins = [1, 2, 5], amount = 11` -> Output: `3` (5 + 5 + 1). Sample Input: `coins = [2], amount = 3` -> Output: `-1`. Time Complexity: O(amount * len(coins)). Space Complexity: O(amount).
key_points: Unbounded knapsack dynamic programming formulation
Base case: `dp[0] = 0`; all other amounts initialized to `float('inf')`
Transition: `dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - coin] + 1)`
Time Complexity: O(amount * len(coins)); Space Complexity: O(amount)
common_mistakes: Greedy approach (always picking largest coin) fails on non-canonical systems like `coins=[1, 3, 4], amount=6` (greedy picks 4+1+1=3 coins; optimal is 3+3=2 coins)
Initializing `dp` with 0 instead of infinity, causing incorrect min comparisons
Forgetting to check if `dp[amount]` is unreachable before returning
follow_up_questions: How does the recurrence change if you need to count the total number of combinations (Coin Change 2)?
Why must coin iteration be outer in Coin Change 2 to avoid counting permutations?

questions.question: Write a Python function to merge all overlapping intervals in a collection.
questions.reference_answer:
Sort intervals by their starting times. Then iterate through intervals and merge with the previous interval if overlap occurs:

```python
def merge_intervals(intervals: list[list[int]]) -> list[list[int]]:
    if not intervals:
        return []
    intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    merged = [intervals[0]]
    for curr in intervals[1:]:
        prev = merged[-1]
        if curr[0] <= prev[1]:
            # Overlapping intervals: extend end boundary
            prev[1] = max(prev[1], curr[1])
        else:
            # Non-overlapping: append new interval
            merged.append(curr)
    return merged
```

Sample Input: `[[1, 3], [2, 6], [8, 10], [15, 18]]` -> Output: `[[1, 6], [8, 10], [15, 18]]`. Sample Input: `[[1, 4], [4, 5]]` -> Output: `[[1, 5]]`. Sorting takes O(n log n) time, and linear merging pass takes O(n). Total Time: O(n log n). Space: O(n) for output.
key_points: Sort intervals primarily by start time `intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])`
Compare `curr[0] <= prev[1]` to detect overlap
Extend end boundary: `prev[1] = max(prev[1], curr[1])`
Time Complexity: O(n log n); Space Complexity: O(n)
common_mistakes: Forgetting to sort intervals before merging
Setting `prev[1] = curr[1]` instead of `max(prev[1], curr[1])`, failing when an interval is completely swallowed (e.g., `[1, 5]` and `[2, 3]`)
Assuming adjacent intervals like `[1, 4]` and `[4, 5]` do not overlap (they share point 4)
follow_up_questions: How do you insert a new interval into an already sorted list of non-overlapping intervals in O(n) time?

questions.question: Write a Python function to find the K most frequent elements in an array in O(n log k) time or better.
questions.reference_answer:
Method 1 (Min-Heap of size K in O(n log k)):
```python
import heapq
from collections import Counter

def top_k_frequent_heap(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    count = Counter(nums)
    # Min-heap stores (frequency, num)
    return heapq.nlargest(k, count.keys(), key=count.get)
```

Method 2 (Bucket Sort in O(n) linear time):
```python
def top_k_frequent_bucket(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    count = Counter(nums)
    buckets = [[] for _ in range(len(nums) + 1)]
    for num, freq in count.items():
        buckets[freq].append(num)
    result = []
    for freq in range(len(buckets) - 1, 0, -1):
        for num in buckets[freq]:
            result.append(num)
            if len(result) == k:
                return result
    return result
```
Sample Input: `nums = [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], k = 2` -> Output: `[1, 2]`. Bucket sort runs in O(n) time and O(n) space.
key_points: Frequency hash map via `Counter` counts occurrences in O(n)
Heap approach maintains min-heap of size K in O(n log k)
Bucket Sort uses frequencies as indices (`buckets[freq]`) to achieve O(n) linear time
Iterates buckets backwards from highest frequency to collect top K
common_mistakes: Sorting the entire dictionary by frequency taking O(u log u) time where u is unique keys
Not handling case where array contains all unique elements
Creating buckets of size `k` instead of size `len(nums) + 1`
follow_up_questions: When is Bucket Sort preferred over Min-Heap, and what are their relative memory trade-offs?

questions.question: Write a Python function to solve the Course Schedule problem (detecting cycles in prerequisites) using Kahn's Topological Sort.
questions.reference_answer:
To finish all courses, the prerequisite graph must be a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). Kahn's Algorithm (BFS using in-degrees) detects cycles:

```python
from collections import deque

def can_finish_courses(num_courses: int, prerequisites: list[list[int]]) -> bool:
    adj = [[] for _ in range(num_courses)]
    in_degree = [0] * num_courses
    for dest, src in prerequisites:
        adj[src].append(dest)
        in_degree[dest] += 1
    queue = deque([i for i in range(num_courses) if in_degree[i] == 0])
    processed = 0
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        processed += 1
        for neighbor in adj[node]:
            in_degree[neighbor] -= 1
            if in_degree[neighbor] == 0:
                queue.append(neighbor)
    return processed == num_courses
```

If the total processed nodes equals `num_courses`, topological order is valid (no cycle). If `processed < num_courses`, a dependency cycle exists. Sample Input: `num_courses = 2, prerequisites = [[1, 0]]` -> `True`. Sample Input: `prerequisites = [[1, 0], [0, 1]]` -> `False`. Time: O(V + E). Space: O(V + E).
key_points: Model courses as directed edges `src -> dest`
In-degree tracks number of remaining prerequisite courses
Enqueue all nodes with `in_degree == 0` (courses with no prerequisites)
If `processed == num_courses`, DAG has no cycle and all courses can be finished
common_mistakes: Reversing edge direction `[dest, src]` causing incorrect in-degree counts
Using DFS cycle detection without 3-state coloring (`unvisited`, `visiting`, `visited`), failing to detect back-edges
Assuming disconnected graphs always contain cycles
follow_up_questions: How do you return the actual course order (Course Schedule II)?
How does 3-color DFS cycle detection work on directed graphs?
